interviewQuestions.q: Why should retrieval be evaluated separately from generation in a RAG system?
interviewQuestions.a: Because a wrong answer can come from either stage and the fixes are different. If the right passage was never retrieved, prompt changes will not help; if it was retrieved but the model ignored or contradicted it, retrieval tuning will not help. Measuring recall at k on labelled queries first tells you which stage to work on.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you test for hallucination?
interviewQuestions.a: Define it concretely for the product, usually claims not supported by the provided sources. Build cases including questions the sources cannot answer, check whether each claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved context using human review and a calibrated judge or entailment check, verify citations actually support the cited claim, and track the unsupported-claim rate per category. Expect the rate to be reduced, not eliminated, and design the product for that.

interviewQuestions.q: How would you test an agent that uses tools?
interviewQuestions.a: Test the outcome: did it complete the task correctly. Test the trajectory: sensible tool choice, valid arguments, no unnecessary or repeated calls, correct handling of tool errors. Test boundaries: it should not take actions outside its permissions, and destructive actions should need confirmation. Run tasks several times because behaviour varies, use sandboxed or mocked tools, and include injected instructions in tool results.

interviewQuestions.q: What would you check when testing an MCP server?
interviewQuestions.a: That tool schemas and descriptions are accurate, inputs are validated server-side, authorisation is enforced for each call rather than trusting the client, errors are returned clearly without leaking secrets, side-effecting tools are clearly identified, and outputs that may contain untrusted content are treated as data. I would also test behaviour on malformed requests and timeouts.

interviewQuestions.q: What is hybrid search and when does it help?
interviewQuestions.a: Combining lexical search such as BM25 with vector similarity, usually by merging the ranked lists, for example with reciprocal rank fusion. It helps when queries contain exact terms like product codes, names or error messages that embeddings may handle poorly, while vectors handle paraphrase. I would verify the benefit on a labelled query set rather than assume it.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you keep evaluation results comparable when models are non-deterministic?
interviewQuestions.a: Fix everything you control: dataset, prompts, model version identifier, retrieval index and grader. Run each configuration multiple times and report the spread, compare per category, and treat small differences as noise unless they exceed run-to-run variation. Do not rely on sampling parameters to remove variation, since some current models only accept their default settings.

sampleProject.title: Red-team assessment of a sandboxed agent
sampleProject.description: Build or use a deliberately vulnerable sandbox agent with a RAG source and two tools. Under a written scope, test direct and indirect prompt injection, system prompt leakage, data exfiltration through tool calls and unsafe actions. Report findings with severity and reproduction steps, propose layered mitigations, implement one, and show the regression tests before and after.

interviewQuestions.q: What is indirect prompt injection and why is it hard to fix?
interviewQuestions.a: It is when instructions arrive through content the model processes rather than from the user, such as a web page, email, document or tool result. The model sees instructions and data in the same context and cannot reliably tell them apart, so there is no complete fix in the prompt alone. Mitigations are layered: treat such content as untrusted, limit the agent's permissions, require confirmation for consequential actions, filter or isolate untrusted content, and monitor.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you scope an AI red-team engagement?
interviewQuestions.a: Get written authorisation from the system owner, define which systems, environments, accounts and techniques are in scope, what is out of scope such as production data or third-party services, how sensitive outputs are stored and who sees them, how to stop if something goes wrong, and how findings are reported. I do not test systems I am not authorised to test, including public AI services outside their published programmes.

interviewQuestions.q: How do you rate the severity of an AI finding?
interviewQuestions.a: Consider impact if exploited, such as data exposure, unauthorised actions or harmful content reaching users, how easy and reliable the attack is, required access, and how many users it could affect. Because attacks may succeed only some of the time, I report the success rate over repeated attempts. A reliable injection that triggers a destructive tool call is far more severe than an occasional mild policy violation.

interviewQuestions.q: An agent can send emails. What would you test?
interviewQuestions.a: Whether injected content in incoming emails or documents can make it send messages, forward data or change recipients; whether sending requires user confirmation; whether it respects recipient restrictions; whether it leaks system prompts or other users' data; and how it behaves when tools return errors or unexpected content. I would also check logging so misuse can be detected.

interviewQuestions.q: Why is red teaming not sufficient on its own?
interviewQuestions.a: It shows that certain attacks worked or failed in the time available; it does not prove the absence of vulnerabilities. It needs to sit alongside threat modelling, secure design such as least privilege, systematic evaluations, regression tests from findings and production monitoring.
